west side, Simeon <hi type="italic">shall have</hi> a <hi type="italic">portion.</hi> <hi type="super">25</hi> And by the border of Simeon, from the east side unto the west side, Issachar a <hi type="italic">portion.</hi> <hi type="super">26</hi> And by the border of Issachar, from the east side unto the west side, Zebulun a <hi type="italic">portion.</hi> <hi type="super">27</hi> And by the border of Zebulun, from the east side unto the west side, Gad a <hi type="italic">portion.</hi> <hi type="super">28</hi> And by the border of Gad, at the south side southward, the border shall be even from Tamar <hi type="italic">unto</hi> the waters of strife <hi type="italic">in</hi> Kadesh, <hi type="italic">and</hi> to the river toward the great sea. <hi type="super">29</hi> This <hi type="italic">is</hi> the land which ye shall divide by lot unto the tribes of Israel for inheritance, and these <hi type="italic">are</hi> their portions, saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> . <hi type="super">30</hi> And these <hi type="italic">are</hi> the goings out of the city on the north side, four thousand and five hundred measures. <div eID="gen19306" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19307" type="x-p"/> We have here a very short and ready way taken for the dividing of the land among the twelve tribes, not so tedious and so far about as the way that was taken in Joshua's time; for in the distribution of spiritual and heavenly blessings there is not that danger of murmuring and quarrelling that there is in the participation of the temporal blessings. When God gave to the labourers every one his penny those that were uneasy at it were soon put to silence with, <hi type="italic">May I not do what I will with my own?</hi> And such is the equal distribution here among the tribes. In this distribution of the land we may observe, 1. That it differs very much from the division of it in Joshua's time, and agrees not with the order of their birth, nor with that of their blessing by Jacob or Moses. Simeon here is not <hi type="italic">divided</hi> in Jacob, nor is Zebulun a <hi type="italic">haven of ships,</hi> a plain intimation that it is not so much to be understood literally as spiritually, though the mystery of it is very much hidden from us. In gospel times old things have passed away; <hi type="italic">behold, all things have become new.</hi> The Israel of God is cast into a new method. 2. That the tribe of Dan, which was last provided for in the first division of Canaan (<reference osisRef="Josh.19.40">Josh. xix. 40</reference>), is first provided for here, <reference osisRef="Ezek.48.1">v. 1</reference>. Thus in the gospel the last shall be first, <reference osisRef="Matt.19.30">Matt. xix. 30</reference>. God, in the dispensation of his grace, does not follow the same method that he does in the disposals of his providence. But Dan had now his portion thereabouts where he had only one city before, northward, on the border of Damascus, and furthest of all from the sanctuary, because that tribe had revolted to idolatry. 3. That all the ten tribes that were carried away by the king of Assyria, as well as the two tribes that were long afterwards carried to Babylon, have their allotment in this visionary land, which some think had its accomplishment in the particular persons and families of those tribes who returned with Judah and Benjamin, of which we find many instances in Ezra and Nehemiah; and it is probable that there were returns of many more afterwards at several times, which are not recorded; and the Jews having Galilee, and other parts, that had been the possessions of the ten tribes, put into their hands, in common with them, they enjoyed them. Grotius says, If the ten tribes had repented and returned to God, as the <hi type="italic">chief fathers of Judah and Benjamin did, and the priests and Levites</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezra.1.5">Ezra i. 5</reference>), they would have fared as those two tribes did, but they forfeited the benefit of this glorious prophecy by sin. However, we believe it has its designed accomplishment in the establishment and enlargement of the gospel church, and the happy settlement of all those who are Israelites indeed in the sure and sweet enjoyment of the privileges of the new covenant, in which there is enough for all and enough for each. 4. That every tribe in this visionary distribution had its particular lot assigned it by a divine appointment; for it was never the intention of the gospel to pluck up the hedge of property and lay all in common; it was in a way of charity, not of legal right, that the first Christians had all things common (<reference osisRef="Acts.2.44">Acts ii. 44</reference>), and many precepts of the gospel suppose that every man should know his own. We must not only acknowledge, but acquiesce in, the hand of God appointing us our lot, and be well pleased with it, believing it fittest for us. <hi type="italic">He shall choose our inheritance for us,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.47.4">Ps. xlvii. 4</reference>. 5. That the tribes lay contiguous. By <hi type="italic">the border</hi> of one tribe was <hi type="italic">the portion</hi> of another, all in a row, in exact order, so that, like stones in an arch, they fixed, and strengthened, and wedged in one another. <hi type="italic">Behold how good and how pleasant a thing it is for brethren</hi> thus <hi type="italic">to dwell together!</hi> It was a figure of the communion of churches and saints under the gospel-government; thus, though they are many, yet they are one, and should hold together in holy love and mutual assistance. 6. That the lot of Reuben, which before lay at a distance beyond Jordan, now lies next to Judah, and next but one to the sanctuary; for the scandal he lay under, for which he was told <hi type="italic">he should not excel,</hi> began by this time to wear off. What has turned to the reproach of any person or people ought not to be remembered for ever, but should at length be kindly forgotten. 7. That the sanctuary was <hi type="italic">in the midst</hi> of them. There were seven tribes to the north of it and the Levites, the prince's, and the city's portion, with that of five tribes more, to the south of it; so that it was, as it ought to be, <hi type="italic">in the heart of the kingdom,</hi> that it might diffuse its benign influences to the whole, and might be the centre of their unity. The tribes that lay most remote from each other would meet there in a mutual acquaintance and fellowship. Those of the same parish or congregation, though dispersed, and having no occasion otherwise to know each other, yet by meeting statedly to worship God together should have their hearts knit to each other in holy love. 8. That where the sanctuary was the priests were: <hi type="italic">For them, even for the priests, shall this holy oblation be,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.48.10">v. 10</reference>. As, on the one hand, this denotes honour and comfort to ministers, that what is given for their support and maintenance is reckoned <hi type="italic">a holy oblation to the Lord,</hi> so it intimates their duty, which is that, since they are appointed and maintained for the service of the sanctuary, they ought to <hi type="italic">attend continually to this very thing,</hi> to reside on their cures. Those that live upon the altar must serve at the altar, not take the wages to themselves and devolve the work upon others; but how can they serve the altar, his altar they live upon, if they do not live near it? 9. Those priests had the priests' share of these lands that had approved themselves faithful to God in times of trial (<reference osisRef="Ezek.48.11">v. 11</reference>): <hi type="italic">It shall be for the sons of Zadok,</hi> who, it seems, had signalized themselves in some critical juncture, and <hi type="italic">went not astray</hi> when the <hi type="italic">children of Israel,</hi> and the other Levites, went astray. God will put honour upon those who keep their integrity in times of general apostasy, and he has special favours in reserve for them. Those are swimming upwards, and so they will find at last, that are swimming against the stream. 10. The land which was appropriated to the ministers of the sanctuary might by no means be alienated. It was in the nature of the <hi type="italic">first-fruits of the land,</hi> and was therefore <hi type="italic">holy to the Lord;</hi> and, though the priests and Levites had both the use of it and the inheritance of it to them and their heirs, yet they might not <hi type="italic">sell it nor exchange it,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.48.14">v. 14</reference>. It is sacrilege to convert that to other uses which is dedicated to God. 11. The land allotted for the city and its suburbs is called a <hi type="italic">profane place</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.48.15">v. 15</reference>), or <hi type="italic">common;</hi> not but that the city was a holy city above other cities, for the Lord was there, but, in comparison with the sanctuary, it was a profane place. Yet it is too often true in the worst sense that great cities, even those which, like this, have the sanctuary near them, are profane places, and it ought to be deeply lamented. It was the complaint of old, <hi type="italic">From Jerusalem has profaneness gone forth into all the land,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.23.15">Jer. xxiii. 15</reference>. 12. The city is made to be exactly square, and the suburbs extending themselves equally on all sides, as the Levites' cities did in the first division of the land (<reference osisRef="Ezek.48.16-Ezek.48.17">v. 16, 17</reference>), which, never being literally fulfilled in any city, intimates that it is to be understood spiritually of the beauty and stability of the gospel church, that <hi type="italic">city of the living God,</hi> which is formed according to the wisdom and counsel of God, and is made firm and immovable by his promise. 13. Whereas, before, the inhabitants of Jerusalem were principally of Judah and Benjamin, in whose tribe it lay, now the head city lies not in the particular lot of any of the tribes, but <hi type="italic">those that serve the city,</hi> and bear office in it, <hi type="italic">shall serve it out of all the tribes of Israel,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.48.19">v. 19</reference>. The most eminent men must be picked out of all the tribes of Israel for the service of the city, because many eyes were upon it, and there was great resort to it from all parts of the nation and from other nations. Those that live in the city are said to serve the city, for, wherever we are, we must study to be serviceable to the place, some way or other, according as our capacity is. They must not come out of the tribes of Israel to the city to take their ease, and enjoy their pleasures, but to serve the city, to do all the good they can there, and in so doing they would have a good influence upon the country too. 14. Care was taken that those who applied themselves to public business in the city, as well as in the sanctuary, should have an honourable comfortable maintenance; lands are appointed, <hi type="italic">the increase</hi> whereof <hi type="italic">shall be food unto those that serve the city,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.48.18">v. 18</reference>. Who goes a warfare at his own charges? Magistrates, that attend the service of the state, as well as ministers, that attend the service of the church, should have all due encouragement and support in so doing; and <hi type="italic">for this cause pay we tribute also.</hi> 15. The prince had a lot for himself, suited to the dignity of his high station (<reference osisRef="Ezek.48.21">v. 21</reference>); we took an account of it before, <reference osisRef="Ezek.45.1-Ezek.45.25">ch. xlv.</reference> He was seated near the sanctuary, where the testimony of Israel was, and near the city, where the <hi type="italic">thrones of judgment</hi> were, that he might be a protection to both and might see the that duty of both was carefully and faithfully done; and herein he was a minister of God for good to the whole community. Christ is the church's prince, that defends it on every side, and creates a defense; nay, he is himself a defence upon all its glory and encompasses it with his favour. 16. As Judah had his lot next the sanctuary on one side, so Benjamin had, of all the tribes, his lot nearest to it on the other side, which honour was reserved for those who adhered to the house of David and the temple at Jerusalem when the other ten tribes went astray from both. It is enough if treachery and apostasy, upon repentance, he pardoned, but constancy and fidelity shall be rewarded and preferred.
entries.45f7611f8606a6dc88828d1881a3083e35f02b75: <div eID="gen19307" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Plan of the City. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 574.)</title> <div sID="gen19308" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">31</hi> And the gates of the city <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> after the names of the tribes of Israel: three gates northward; one gate of Reuben, one gate of Judah, one gate of Levi. <hi type="super">32</hi> And at the east side four thousand and five hundred: and three gates; and one gate of Joseph, one gate of Benjamin, one gate of <reference osisRef="Dan.33">Dan.   33</reference> And at the south side four thousand and five hundred measures: and three gates; one gate of Simeon, one gate of Issachar, one gate of Zebulun. <hi type="super">34</hi> At the west side four thousand and five hundred, <hi type="italic">with</hi> their three gates; one gate of Gad, one gate of Asher, one gate of Naphtali. <hi type="super">35</hi> <hi type="italic">It was</hi> round about eighteen thousand <hi type="italic">measures:</hi> and the name of the city from <hi type="italic">that</hi> day <hi type="italic">shall be,</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> there. <div eID="gen19308" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19309" type="x-p"/> We have here a further account of the city that should be built for the metropolis of this glorious land, and to be the receptacle of those who would come from all parts to worship in the sanctuary adjoining. It is nowhere called Jerusalem, nor is the land which we have had such a particular account of the dividing of any where called the land of Canaan; for the old names are forgotten, to intimate that the <hi type="italic">old things are done away, behold all things have become new.</hi> Now, concerning this city, observe here, 1. The measures of its out-lets, and the grounds belonging to it, for its several conveniences; each way its appurtenances extended 4500 <hi type="italic">measures</hi> 18,000 in all, <reference osisRef="Ezek.48.35">v. 35</reference>. But what these measures were is uncertain. It is never said, in all this chapter, whether so many <hi type="italic">reeds</hi> (as our translation determines by inserting that word, <reference osisRef="Ezek.48.8">v. 8</reference>, each reed containing six cubits and span, <reference osisRef="Ezek.40.5">ch. xl. 5</reference>, and why should the measurer appear with the measuring reed in his hand of that length if he did not measure with <hi type="italic">that,</hi> except where it is expressly said he measured by cubits?) or whether, as others think, it is so many cubits, because those are mentioned <reference osisRef="Ezek.45.2">ch. xlv. 2</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ezek.47.3">ch. xlvii. 3</reference>. Yet that makes me incline rather to think that where cubits are not mentioned must be intended so many lengths of the measuring reed. But those who understand it of so many cubits are not agreed whether it be meant of the common cubit, which was half a yard, or the geometrical cubit, which, for better expedition, is supposed to be mostly used in surveying lands, which, some say, contained six cubits, others about three cubits and a half, so making 1000 cubits the same with 1000 paces, that is, an English mile. But our being left at this uncertainty is an intimation that these things are to be understood spiritually, and that what is principally meant is that there is an exact and just proportion observed by Infinite Wisdom in modelling the gospel church, which though now we cannot discern we shall when we come to heaven. 2. The number of its gates. It had twelve gates in all, three on each side, which was very agreeable when it lay four square; and these twelve gates were inscribed to the twelve tribes. Because the city was to be served <hi type="italic">out of all the tribes of Israel</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.48.19">v. 19</reference>) it was fit that each tribe should have its gate; and, Levi being here taken in, to keep to the number twelve Ephraim and Manasseh are made one in Joseph, <reference osisRef="Ezek.48.32">v. 32</reference>. On the north side were the gates of Reuben, Judah, and Levi (<reference osisRef="Ezek.48.31">v. 31</reference>), on the east the gates of Joseph, Benjamin, and Dan (<reference osisRef="Ezek.48.32">v. 32</reference>), on the south the gates of Simeon, Issachar, and Zebulun (<reference osisRef="Ezek.48.33">v. 33</reference>), and on the west the gates of Gad, Asher, and Naphtali, <reference osisRef="Ezek.48.34">v. 34</reference>. Conformable to this, in St. John's vision, the new Jerusalem (for so the holy city is called there, though not here) has <hi type="italic">twelve gates,</hi> three on a side, and on them are written <hi type="italic">the names of the twelve tribes of the children of Israel,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.21.12-Rev.21.13">Rev. xxi. 12, 13</reference>. Note, Into the church of Christ, both militant and triumphant, there is a free access by faith for all that come of every tribe, from every quarter. Christ has <hi type="italic">opened the kingdom of heaven for all believers.</hi> Whoever will may come and <hi type="italic">take of the water of life,</hi> of the tree of life, <hi type="italic">freely.</hi> 3. The name given to this city: <hi type="italic">From that day,</hi> when it shall be newly-erected according to this model, the name of it shall be, not, as before, <hi type="italic">Jerusalem—The vision of peace,</hi> but which is the original of that, and more than equivalent to it, <hi type="italic">Jehovah Shammah—The Lord is there,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.48.35">v. 35</reference>. This intimated, (1.) That the captives, after their return, should have manifest tokens of God's presence with them and his residence among them, both in his ordinances and his providences. They shall have no occasion to ask, as their fathers did, <hi type="italic">Is the Lord among us, or is he not?</hi> for they shall see and say that he is with them of a truth. And then, though their troubles were many and threatening, they were like the bush which burned but was not consumed, because <hi type="italic">the Lord was there.</hi> But when God departed from their temple, when he said, <hi type="italic">Migremus hinc—Let us go hence,</hi> their house was soon <hi type="italic">left unto them desolate.</hi> Being no longer his, it was not much longer theirs. (2.) That the gospel-church should likewise have the presence of God in it, though not in the <hi type="italic">Shechinah,</hi> as of old, yet in a token of it no less sure, that of his Spirit. Where the gospel is faithfully preached, gospel ordinances are duly administered, and God is worshipped in the name of Jesus Christ only, it may truly be said, <hi type="italic">The Lord is there;</hi> for faithful is he that has said, and he will be as good as his word, <hi type="italic">Lo, I am with you always even unto the end of the world. The Lord is there</hi> in his church, to rule and govern it, to protect and defend it, and graciously to accept and own his sincere worshippers, and to be <hi type="italic">nigh unto them in all that they call upon him for.</hi> This should engage us to keep close to the communion of saints, for <hi type="italic">the Lord is there;</hi> and then whither shall we go to better ourselves? Nay, it is true of every good Christian; he dwells in God, and God in him; whatever soul has in it a living principle of grace, it may be truly said, <hi type="italic">The Lord is There.</hi> (3.) That the glory and happiness of heaven should consist chiefly in this, that <hi type="italic">the Lord is there.</hi> St. John's representation of that blessed state does indeed far exceed this in many respects. That is all gold, and pearls, and precious stones; it is much larger than this, and much brighter, for it <hi type="italic">needs not the light of the sun.</hi> But, in making the presence of God the principal matter of its bliss, they both agree. There the happiness of the glorified saints is made to be that <hi type="italic">God himself shall be with them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rev.21.3">Rev. xxi. 3</reference>), that <hi type="italic">he who sits on the throne shall dwell among them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.7.15">Rev. vii. 15</reference>. And here it is made to crown the bliss of this holy city that <hi type="italic">the Lord is there.</hi> Let us therefore give all diligence to make sure to ourselves a place in that city, that we may be <hi type="italic">for ever with the Lord.</hi>  <chapter eID="Ezek.48"/> <div eID="gen19309" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen18363" osisID="Ezek" type="book"/>

entries.199c35c7ad250bd4ed0788197b5fea5da72854f7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11912"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 48</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ezek.48.1-Ezek.48.35">Eze 48:1-35</reference>. Allotment of the Land to the Several Tribes.</title> <div sID="gen21517" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11912"/><hi type="bold">1. Dan--</hi>The lands are divided into portions of ideal exactness, running alongside of each other, the whole breadth from west to east, standing in a common relation to the temple in the center: seven tribes' portions on the north, five in the smaller division in the south. The portions of the city, the temple, the prince, and the priesthood, are in the middle, not within the boundaries of any tribe, all alike having a common interest in them. Judah has the place of honor next the center on the north, Benjamin the corresponding place of honor next the center on the south; because of the adherence of these two to the temple ordinances and to the house of David for so long, when the others deserted them. Dan, on the contrary, so long locally and morally semi-heathen (<reference osisRef="Judg.18.1-Judg.18.31">Jud 18:1-31</reference>), is to have the least honorable place, at the extreme north. For the same reason, St. John (<reference osisRef="Rev.7.5-Rev.7.8">Re 7:5-8</reference>) omits Dan altogether. <div eID="gen21517" type="x-p"/>
entries.80c2c091be1e0e0b049912eb49f1ee35f3ed7d08: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11913"/><div sID="gen21518" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11913"/><hi type="bold">3. Asher--</hi>a tribe of which no one of note is mentioned in the Old Testament. In the New Testament one is singled out of it, the prophetess Anna. <div eID="gen21518" type="x-p"/>
entries.78945de5e926862175854e75b8db390a833c7cd8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11914"/><div sID="gen21519" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11914"/><hi type="bold">4. Manasseh--</hi>The intercourse and unity between the two and a half tribes east of the Jordan, and the nine and a half west of it, had been much kept up by the splitting of Manasseh, causing the visits of kinsmen one to the other from both sides of the Jordan. There shall be no need for this in the new order of things. <div eID="gen21519" type="x-p"/>
entries.d221578672904ef7c1b42d4c0dad9a92a833a34a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11915"/><div sID="gen21520" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11915"/><hi type="bold">5. Ephraim--</hi>This tribe, within its two dependent tribes, Manasseh and Benjamin, for upwards of four hundred years under the judges held the pre-eminence. <div eID="gen21520" type="x-p"/>
entries.7bfdc27376d8fe58021333a0f9c82a1314c67e4b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11916"/><div sID="gen21521" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11916"/><hi type="bold">6. Reuben--</hi>doomed formerly for incest and instability "not to excel" (<reference osisRef="Gen.49.4">Ge 49:4</reference>). So no distinguished prophet, priest, or king had come from it. Of it were the notorious Dathan and Abiram, the mutineers. A pastoral and Bedouin character marked it and Gad (<reference osisRef="Judg.5.16">Jud 5:16</reference>). <div eID="gen21521" type="x-p"/>
entries.191e6764de9972bc3fa9f91c66286611799a5efa: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11917"/><div sID="gen21522" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11917"/>15-17. The five thousand rods, apportioned to the city out of the twenty-five thousand square, are to be laid off in a square of four thousand five hundred, with the two hundred fifty all around for suburbs.<div eID="gen21522" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21523" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">profane--</hi>that is, not strictly sacred as the sacerdotal portions, but applied to secular uses. <div eID="gen21523" type="x-p"/>
entries.e13c1585471acecee1a02582d44ead45c52baa43: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11918"/><div sID="gen21524" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11918"/><hi type="bold">24. Benjamin--</hi>Compare Jacob's prophecy (<reference osisRef="Gen.49.27">Ge 49:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.33.12">De 33:12</reference>). It alone with Judah had been throughout loyal to the house of David, so its prowess at the "night" of the national history was celebrated as well as in the "morning." <div eID="gen21524" type="x-p"/>
entries.a63d299c9d92384437bba1be1e60ed966f0d6a36: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11919"/><div sID="gen21525" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11919"/><hi type="bold">25. Simeon--</hi>omitted in the blessing of Moses in <reference osisRef="Deut.33.1-Deut.33.29">De 33:1-29</reference>, perhaps because of the Simeonite "prince," who at Baal-peor led the Israelites in their idolatrous whoredoms with Midian (<reference osisRef="Num.25.14">Nu 25:14</reference>). <div eID="gen21525" type="x-p"/>
entries.bba58a1c597e4656be26bc931cdd8197ad02545b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11920"/><div sID="gen21526" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11920"/><hi type="bold">26. Issachar--</hi>Its ancient portion had been on the plain of Esdraelon. Compared (<reference osisRef="Gen.49.14">Ge 49:14</reference>) to "a strong ass crouching between two burdens," that is, tribute and tillage; never meddling with wars except in self-defense. <div eID="gen21526" type="x-p"/>
entries.01c9de3d51bc55620683ef514b35487d2be392e0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11921"/><div sID="gen21527" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11921"/><hi type="bold">31. gates--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Rev.21.12">Re 21:12</reference>, &c.). The twelve gates bear the names of the twelve tribes to imply that all are regarded as having an interest in it. <div eID="gen21527" type="x-p"/>
entries.f499e0b140e505d4fdebe3f62ce602f254102f68: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11922"/><div sID="gen21528" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11922"/><hi type="bold">35. Lord is there--</hi>Jehovah-Shammah. Not that the city will be called so in mere name, but that the reality will be best expressed by this descriptive title (<reference osisRef="Jer.3.17">Jr 3:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.33.16">33:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.2.10">Zec 2:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.21.3">Re 21:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.22.3">22:3</reference>). <chapter eID="Ezek.48"/><div eID="gen21528" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen19699" osisID="Ezek" type="book"/>

entries.7c1a925005b140fa46a53c79f8ce43002bc0b335: <div eID="gen32666" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen32667" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen32667" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32668" type="x-p"/> This chapter contains a description of the several portions of the land belonging to each tribe, together with the portion allotted to the sanctuary, city, suburb, and prince, vv. 1-29; as also the measure and gates of the new city, <reference osisRef="Eze.48.30-Eze.48.35">Eze 48:30-35</reference>. <div eID="gen32668" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32669" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen32669" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32670" type="x-p"/> Now these are the names of the tribes - See the division mentioned <reference osisRef="Num.34.7-Num.34.12">Num 34:7-12</reference>, which casts much light upon this.
entries.a2bf6ea059d11a5196c830aef2cc381a00a97dc9: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen32670" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32671" type="x-p"/> The oblation - This was a portion of land twenty-five thousand cubits in length, by ten thousand broad; in the center of which was the temple, which must be destined for the use of the priests, the Levites, and the prince.
entries.3b20d3b4ea91a7eae2e306f8d3d055d304ac7317: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen32671" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32672" type="x-p"/> And the five thousand that are left - The territory of the Levites was twenty-five thousand square cubits, <reference osisRef="Eze.48.20">Eze 48:20</reference>, But their city was only four thousand five hundred square cubits, see <reference osisRef="Eze.48.13">Eze 48:13</reference> and <reference osisRef="Eze.48.16">Eze 48:16</reference>; there remained, therefore, ten thousand cubits square to be divided, of which five thousand cubits in breadth, by twenty-five thousand in length, on the east and west sides, were reserved for a sort of second city; or for suburbs where laymen might dwell who were employed by those priests and Levites who lodged in the temple and in the city, <reference osisRef="Eze.48.18">Eze 48:18</reference>. And another space of one thousand cubits in breadth, by twenty-five thousand in length, which extended only from north to south, was for fields and gardens appointed for the support of those lay servants. On which we may remark, there was no cultivated land between the portion of the Levites and that of the prince, but only on the east and west sides. See <reference osisRef="Eze.45.6">Eze 45:6</reference>, and the map FF.
entries.d59afabbb2fbe56e96d8a520667eb9fab60f5d64: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen32672" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32673" type="x-p"/> And the residue - for the prince - His portion was alongside that of the Levites, from west to east; these were on each side twenty-five thousand cubits in length, from the east to the west. by twelve thousand five hundred cubits in breadth from north to south. The space both above and below was equal, between the tribe of Judah and that of Benjamin to north and south; and the portion of the Levites, which had Judah and Benjamin to the north and south, and the portion of the prince to the east and to the west. See the map.
entries.63d540e4b0084e7c26fca2198f6414ec0110c495: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen32673" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32674" type="x-p"/> From Tamar - in Kadesh - The former was on the south of the Dead Sea; and the latter, or Kadesh-Barnea, was still farther south, and at the extremity of the portion of Gad, which was the most southern tribe, as Dan was the most northern.
entries.6e571422cbbfea5c9f89b52d79547a069e7a1912: <hi type="bold">Verse 30</hi> <div eID="gen32674" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32675" type="x-p"/> These are the goings out - Each of the four sides of the city was four thousand five hundred cubits long. There were three gates on each side, as mentioned below; and the whole circumference of the city was eighteen thousand cubits. See the map, plan B. dddd. <div eID="gen32675" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32676" type="x-p"/> The rector of New Haven College, in New England, supposes the preceding representations to refer to the happy state of the Church in what is called the Millennium. Leaving this period out of the question, the following observations are worthy of notice: - "The Jews, for whom this vision was intended, would conceive their country to be divided to the twelve tribes, in lots of a regular and mathematical form; and not confused or intermixed, as in Joshua's time. Their city laid out larger than before; and exactly foursquare, with regular suburbs; the temple and appendages much more commodious for their sacrifices, and the habitations of the priests and Levites regularly formed round about the temple. So that this whole plan of the division of the country, laying out of the city, temple, and all the appendages, appears to be perfectly regular and uniform, as if it were drawn all at one time, and by one hand, who had power to effect it; and therefore conveyed to the Jews the most complete idea they were capable of conceiving of the most perfect church, commonwealth, city, temple, and conveniences, for Divine worship. <div eID="gen32676" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32677" type="x-p"/> I. The Holy Land, as described chap. 47 and 48, according to the original grant, being about two hundred and fifty miles long, north and south, and about one hundred and fifty miles wide, is divided, by parallel lines east and west, to the twelve tribes, each of them having a portion twenty miles wide. Only between Judah and Benjamin there is a holy portion near ten miles wide; in the middle of which is the holy oblation, twenty-five thousand cubits; that is, about ten miles square for the priests, Levites, city, and temple, <reference osisRef="Eze.45.1">Eze 45:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eze.48.8">Eze 48:8</reference>; the two ends are for the prince, <reference osisRef="Eze.45.7">Eze 45:7</reference>, etc. <div eID="gen32677" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32678" type="x-p"/> II. The holy oblation, lying in the middle of the holy portion, is twenty-five thousand cubits square, which is near ten miles; of which ten thousand cubits, or four miles, are taken off from the north side for a habitation for the priests, and as much for the Levites on the south side, <reference osisRef="Eze.45.4">Eze 45:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eze.45.5">Eze 45:5</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Eze.48.20">Eze 48:20</reference>; and five thousand cubits in the middle for the city portion, <reference osisRef="Eze.45.6">Eze 45:6</reference>; in the middle of which is the city, four thousand five hundred cubits square, which is nearly two miles, <reference osisRef="Eze.48.15">Eze 48:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eze.48.16">Eze 48:16</reference>. Round about this is left two hundred and fifty cubits, near thirty rods, for suburbs, <reference osisRef="Eze.48.17">Eze 48:17</reference>. The remaining ten thousand cubits on the east side, and the ten thousand cubits on the west side, are for the profit of those who serve the city, out of all the tribes, <reference osisRef="Eze.48.18">Eze 48:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eze.48.19">Eze 48:19</reference>. The sanctuary is in the midst of the city, <reference osisRef="Eze.48.8">Eze 48:8</reference>. <div eID="gen32678" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32679" type="x-p"/> III. The sanctuary or temple, and its appendages, were entirely surrounded with a wall six cubits high and six cubits thick, <reference osisRef="Eze.40.5">Eze 40:5</reference>; and five hundred cubits long on each side, <reference osisRef="Eze.42.15">Eze 42:15</reference>, etc., and <reference osisRef="Eze.45.2">Eze 45:2</reference>. In the middle square stands the temple, which was surrounded by a wall one hundred cubits long on each side, <reference osisRef="Eze.41.13">Eze 41:13</reference>, and six cubits thick, <reference osisRef="Eze.41.5">Eze 41:5</reference>. The side-chambers on the outside four cubits, <reference osisRef="Eze.41.5">Eze 41:5</reference>. The Holy of Holies, at the west end, was twenty cubits square on the inside, <reference osisRef="Eze.41.4">Eze 41:4</reference>. The holy place or outer court at the east end, was forty cubits, <reference osisRef="Eze.41.12">Eze 41:12</reference>. The length of the porch on the north side was twenty cubits; the breadth was eleven cubits, <reference osisRef="Eze.40.49">Eze 40:49</reference>; and the width of the separate place on the south side twenty cubits. On each side of the temple, towards the four gates in the outer wall, stood two courts, eight in the whole, each one hundred cubits square, <reference osisRef="Eze.40.19">Eze 40:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eze.40.23">Eze 40:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eze.40.27">Eze 40:27</reference>. In each of these were thirty-six little chambers or buildings, about six cubits square, viz., six at the entrance of the gate, <reference osisRef="Eze.40.7">Eze 40:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eze.40.17">Eze 40:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eze.40.20">Eze 40:20</reference>, etc., and thirty on the pavement, <reference osisRef="Eze.40.17">Eze 40:17</reference>, etc., which were for lodgings for the priests, for hanging up their garments, and their part of the sacrifices, <reference osisRef="Eze.42.13">Eze 42:13</reference>." <div eID="gen32679" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32680" type="x-p"/> Calmet has constructed a map to show the position of the tribes, and the quantum of space each was to possess. As this will give a better view of the subject than any written description can, I have inserted one constructed for this work, which, consulting the places said to be connected with the possessions of the different tribes, shows that the tribes did not all possess the same quantum of space, five of the southern tribes possessing only one half as much as those of the north.
entries.709a58c07412b3d818cf00b96197bec7feeef6fe: <hi type="bold">Verse 35</hi> <div eID="gen32680" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32681" type="x-p"/> The name of the city from that day shall be, The Lord is there - It would have been better to have retained the original words: - יהוה שמה <div eID="gen32681" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32682" type="x-p"/> Yehovah Shammah. <div eID="gen32682" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32683" type="x-p"/> This is an allusion to the shechinah, or symbol of the Divine Presence, which was in the first, but most certainly was not in the second temple; but Ezekiel tells us that the Divine Presence should be in the city of which he speaks; and should be there so fully and so powerfully, that it should give name to the city itself; and that the very name, Jehovah shammah, should remind all men of the supereminently glorious Being who had condescended to make this city his habitation. <div eID="gen32683" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32684" type="x-p"/> Two points must be considered here: - <div eID="gen32684" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32685" type="x-p"/> 1. That the prophet intended that, when they should be restored, they should build the temple, and divide the land as he here directs, if the thing could be found to be practicable. <div eID="gen32685" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32686" type="x-p"/> 2. That he had another temple, another holy city, another Promised Land, in view. The land of Immanuel, the city of the New Jerusalem; and his temple, the Christian Church, which is the house of the living God, <reference osisRef="1Tim.3.15">1Tim 3:15</reference>, in which the presence of Christ shall ever be found; and all its inhabitants, all that believe on his name, shall be temples of the Holy Ghost. Nor can there be any reasonable doubt that the prophet here, by the Spirit of God, not only points out the return of the Israelites from the Babylonish captivity, and what was to befall them previously to the advent of Jesus Christ; but also the glorious spread of the Gospel in the earth, and the final conversion of the tribes of Israel by the preaching of that Gospel. <div eID="gen32686" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32687" type="x-p"/> In conclusion, I think it necessary to state, that there are but few of the prophets of the Old Testament who have left a more valuable treasure to the Church of God than Ezekiel. It is true, he is in several places obscure; but there is a great proportion of the work that is in the highest degree edifying; and several portions that for the depth of the salvation predicted, and the accuracy and minuteness of the description, have nothing equal to them in the Old Testament Scriptures. On such portions, I have felt it my duty to be very particular, that I might be able to point out spiritual beauties and excellencies in this book which are beyond all praise; while I passed slightly over prophecies and symbols which I did not fully understand; but have left to time, by the fulfillment of the events, to prove to successive generations with what heavenly wisdom this much neglected prophet has spoken. And I take this opportunity to recommend this book to the serious perusal of every pious man; and while he wonders at the extent of the wisdom by which Ezekiel has fathomed the depth of so many Divine mysteries, let him give God the glory for this additional testimony to the unsearchable riches of Christ, and that plenary salvation which he has purchased for, and freely offers to, the vilest of the vile, and to the whole of the descendants of Adam. <div eID="gen32687" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32688" type="x-p"/> Masoretic Notes <div eID="gen32688" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32689" type="x-p"/> Number of verses, 1, 273. <div eID="gen32689" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32690" type="x-p"/> Middle verse, <reference osisRef="Eze.26.1">Eze 26:1</reference>. <div eID="gen32690" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32691" type="x-p"/> Masoretic sections, 29.  <chapter eID="Ezek.48"/> <div eID="gen32691" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen31158" osisID="Ezek" type="book"/>

entries.30c6374c9b6d2be343cac11b3327db1fd80beddc: <reference osisRef="Ezek.48.1-Ezek.48.29">Eze 48:1-29</reference> <div eID="gen15369" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15370" type="x-p"/> The division of the land, like the definition of the boundaries (<reference osisRef="Ezek.47.15">Eze 47:15</reference>), commences in the north, and enumerates the tribes in the order in which they were to receive their inheritances from north to south: first, seven tribes from the northern boundary to the centre of the land (<reference osisRef="Ezek.48.1-Ezek.48.7">Eze 48:1-7</reference>), where the heave for the sanctuary, with the land of the priests and Levites and the city domain, together with the prince’s land on the two sides, was to be set apart (<reference osisRef="Ezek.48.8-Ezek.48.22">Eze 48:8-22</reference>; and secondly, the other five tribes from this to the southern boundary (<reference osisRef="Ezek.48.23-Ezek.48.29">Eze 48:23-29</reference>). Compare the map on Plate IV. <div eID="gen15370" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15371" type="x-p"/> Eze 48:1. <hi type="italic">And these are the names of the tribes: from the north end by the side of the way to Chetlon toward Hamath (and) Hazar-Enon the boundary of Damascus - toward the north by the side of Hamath there shall east side, west side belong to him: Dan one (tribe-lot).</hi> Eze 48:2. <hi type="italic">And on the boundary of Dan from the east side to the west side: Asher one.</hi> Eze 48:3. <hi type="italic">And on the boundary of Asher from the east side to the west side: Naphtali one.</hi> Eze 48:4. <hi type="italic">And on the boundary of Naphtali from the east side to the west side: Manasseh one.</hi> Eze 48:5. <hi type="italic">And on the boundary of Manasseh from the east side to the west side: Ephraim one.</hi> Eze 48:6. <hi type="italic">And on the boundary of Ephraim from the east side to the west side: Reuben one.</hi> Eze 48:7. <hi type="italic">And on the boundary of Reuben from the east side to the west side: Judah one.</hi> Eze 48:8. <hi type="italic">And on the boundary of Judah from the east side to the west side shall be the heave, which ye shall lift (heave) off, five and twenty thousand (rods) in breadth, and the length like every tribe portion from the east side to the west side; and the sanctuary shall be in the midst of it.</hi> Eze 48:9. <hi type="italic">The heave which ye shall lift (heave) for Jehovah shall be five and twenty thousand in length and ten thousand in breadth.</hi> Eze 48:10. <hi type="italic">And to these shall the holy heave belong, to the priests, toward the north, five and twenty thousand; toward the west, breadth ten thousand; toward the east, breadth ten thousand; and toward the south, length five and twenty thousand; and the sanctuary of Jehovah shall be in the middle of it.</hi> Eze 48:11. <hi type="italic">To the priests, whoever is sanctified of the sons of Zadok, who have kept my charge, who have not strayed with the straying of the sons of Israel, as the Levites have strayed,</hi> Eze 48:12. <hi type="italic">To them shall a portion lifted off belong from the heave of the land; a most holy beside the territory of the Levites.</hi> Eze 48:13. <hi type="italic">And the Levites (shall receive) parallel with the territory of the priests five and twenty thousand in length, and in breadth ten thousand; the whole length five and twenty thousand, and (the whole) breadth ten thousand.</hi> Eze 48:14. <hi type="italic">And they shall not sell or exchange any of it, nor shall the first-fruit of the land pass to others; for it is holy to Jehovah.</hi> Eze 48:15. <hi type="italic">And the five thousand which remain in the breadth along the five and twenty thousand are common land for the city for dwellings and for open space; and the city shall be in the centre of it.</hi> Eze 48:16. <hi type="italic">And these are its measures: the north side four thousand five hundred, the south side four thousand five hundred, the east side four thousand five hundred, and the west side four thousand five hundred.</hi> Eze 48:17. <hi type="italic">And the open space of the city shall be toward the north two hundred and fifty, toward the south two hundred and fifty, toward the east two hundred and fifty, and toward the west two hundred and fifty.</hi> Eze 48:18. <hi type="italic">And the remainder in length parallel with the holy heave, ten thousand toward the east and ten thousand toward the west, this shall be beside the holy heave, and its produce shall serve the workmen of the city for food.</hi> Eze 48:19. <hi type="italic">And as for the workmen of the city, they shall cultivate it from all the tribes.</hi> Eze 48:20. <hi type="italic">The whole of the heave is five and twenty thousand by five and twenty thousand; a fourth of the holy heave shall ye take for the possession of the city.</hi> Eze 48:21. <hi type="italic">And the remainder shall belong to the prince on this side and on that side of the holy heave and of the city possession; along the five and twenty thousand of the heave to the eastern boundary, and toward the west along the five and twenty thousand to the western boundary parallel with the tribe portions, it shall belong to the prince; and the holy heave and the sanctuary of the house shall be in the midst.</hi> Eze 48:22. <hi type="italic">Thus from the possession of the Levites (as) from the possession of the city shall that which lies in the midst of what belongs to the prince between the territory of Judah and the territory of Benjamin belong to the prince.</hi> Eze 48:23. <hi type="italic">And the rest of the tribes are from the east side to the west side: Benjamin one.</hi> Eze 48:24. <hi type="italic">And on the boundary of Benjamin from the east side to the west side: Simeon one.</hi> Eze 48:25. <hi type="italic">And on the boundary of Simeon from the east side to the west side: Issachar one.</hi> Eze 48:26. <hi type="italic">And on the boundary of Issachar from the east side to the west side: Zebulon one.</hi> Eze 48:27. <hi type="italic">And on the boundary of Zebulon from the east side to the west side: Gad one.</hi> Eze 48:28. <hi type="italic">And on the boundary of Gad on the south side toward the south, the boundary shall be from Tamar to the water of strife from Kadesh along the brook to the great sea.</hi> Eze 48:29. <hi type="italic">This is the land which ye shall divide by lot for inheritance to the tribes of Israel; these are their portions, is the saying of the Lord Jehovah.</hi> <div eID="gen15371" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15372" type="x-p"/> The new division of the land differs from the former one effected in the time of Joshua, in the first place, in the fact that all the tribe-portions were to extend uniformly across the entire breadth of the land from the eastern boundary to the Mediterranean Sea on the west, so that they were to form parallel tracts of country; whereas in the distribution made in the time of Joshua, several of the tribe-territories covered only half the breadth of the land. For example, Dan received his inheritance on the west of Benjamin; and the territories of half Manasseh and Asher ran up from the northern boundary of Ephraim to the northern boundary of Canaan; while Issachar, Naphtali, and Zebulon received their portions on the east of these; and lastly, Simeon received his possession within the boundaries of the tribe of Judah. And secondly, it also differs from the former, in the fact that not only are all the twelve tribes located in Canaan proper, between the Jordan and the Mediterranean Sea; whereas previously two tribes and a half had received from Moses, at their own request, the conquered land of Bashan and Gilead on the eastern side of the Jordan, so that the land of Canaan could be divided among the remaining nine tribes and a half. But besides this, the central tract of land, about the fifth part of the whole, was separated for the holy heave, the city domain, and the prince’s land, so that only the northern and southern portions, about four-fifths of the whole, remained for distribution among the twelve tribes, seven tribes receiving their hereditary portions to the north of the heave and five to the south, because the heave was so selected that the city with its territory lay near the ancient Jerusalem. - In <reference osisRef="Ezek.48.1-Ezek.48.7">Eze 48:1-7</reference> the seven tribes which were to dwell on the north of the heave are enumerated. The principal points of the northern boundary, viz., the way to Chetlon and Hazar-Enon, the boundary of Damascus, are repeated in <reference osisRef="Ezek.48.1">Eze 48:1</reference> from <reference osisRef="Ezek.47.15">Eze 47:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.47.17">Eze 47:17</reference>, as the starting and terminal points of the northern boundary running from west to east. The words אל־יד חמת fix the northern boundary more precisely in relation to the adjoining territory; and in 'והיוּ  the enumeration of the tribe-lots begins with that of the tribe of Dan, which was to receive its territory against the northern boundary. לו refers to the name דּן which follows, and which Ezekiel already had in his mind. פּאת קדים היּם is constructed <hi type="italic">asyndetôs</hi>; and פּאת is to be repeated in thought before היּם: the east side (and) the west (side) are to belong to it, i.e., the tract of land toward its west and its east side. The words which follow, דּן אחד, are attached in an anacoluthistic manner: “Dan (is to receive) one portion,” for “one shall belong to Dan.” To אחד we are to supply in thought the substantive חבל, tribe-lot, according to Eze 47:13. “The assumption that one tribe was to receive as much as another (vid., <reference osisRef="Ezek.47.14">Eze 47:14</reference>), leads to the conclusion that each tribe-lot was to be taken as a <hi type="italic">monas</hi>” (Kliefoth). In this way the names in <reference osisRef="Ezek.48.2-Ezek.48.7">Eze 48:2-7</reference>, with the constantly repeated אחד, must also be taken. The same form of description is repeated in <reference osisRef="Ezek.48.23-Ezek.48.28">Eze 48:23-28</reference> in the case of the five tribes placed to the south of the heave. - In the order of the several tribe-territories it is impossible to discover any universal principle of arrangement. All that is clear is, that in the case of Dan, Asher, Naphtali, Manasseh, and Ephraim, regard is had to the former position of these tribe-territories as far as the altered circumstances allowed. In the time of the Judges a portion of the Danites had migrated to the north, conquered the city of Laish, and given it the name of Dan, so that from that time forward Dan is generally named as the northern boundary of the land (e.g., as early as <reference osisRef="2Sam.3.10">2Sa 3:10</reference>, and in other passages). Accordingly Dan receives the tract of land along the northern boundary. Asher and Naphtali, which formerly occupied the most northerly portions of the land, follow next. Then comes Manasseh, as half Manasseh had formerly dwelt on the east of Naphtali; and Ephraim joins Manasseh, as it formerly joined the western half of Manasseh. The reason for placing Reuben between Ephraim and Judah appears to be, that Reuben was the first-born of Jacob’s sons. The position of the <hi type="italic">termuah</hi> between Judah and Benjamin is probably connected with the circumstance that Jerusalem formerly stood on the boundary of these two tribes, and so also in the future was to skirt Benjamin with its territory. The other tribes had then to be located on the south of Benjamin; Simeon, whose territory formerly lay to the south; Issachar and Zebulon, for which no room was left in the north; and Gad, which had to be brought over from Gilead to Canaan. <div eID="gen15372" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15373" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Ezek.48.8-Ezek.48.22">Eze 48:8-22</reference>, the <hi type="italic">terumah</hi>, which has already been described in <reference osisRef="Ezek.45.1-Ezek.45.7">Eze 45:1-7</reference> for a different purpose, is more precisely defined: first of all, in <reference osisRef="Ezek.48.8">Eze 48:8</reference>, according to its whole extent - viz. twenty-five thousand rods in breadth (from north to south), and the length the same as any one (= every one) of the tribe-lots, i.e., reaching from the Jordan to the Mediterranean Sea (cf. <reference osisRef="Ezek.45.7">Eze 45:7</reference>). In the centre of this separated territory the sanctuary (the temple) was to stand. בּתוכו, the suffix of which refers <hi type="italic">ad sensum</hi> to חלק instead of תּרוּמה, has not the indefinite meaning “therein,” but signifies “in the centre;” for the priests’ portion, in the middle of which the temple was to stand, occupied the central position between the portion of the Levites and the city possession, as is evident from Eze 48:22. The circumstance that here, as in Eze 45:1., in the division of the <hi type="italic">terumah</hi>, the priests’ portion is mentioned first, then the portion of the Levites, and after this the city possession, proves nothing so far as the local order in which these three portions followed one another is concerned; but the enumeration is regulated by their spiritual significance, so that first of all the most holy land for the temple and priests is defined, then the holy portion of the Levites, and lastly, the common land for the city. The command, that the sanctuary is to occupy the centre of the whole <hi type="italic">terumah</hi>, leads to a more minute description in the first place (<reference osisRef="Ezek.48.9-Ezek.48.12">Eze 48:9-12</reference>) of the priests’ portion, in which the sanctuary was situated, than of the heave to be lifted off for Jehovah. In <reference osisRef="Ezek.48.10">Eze 48:10</reference>, לאלּה, which stands at the head, is explained by לכּהנים which follows. The extent of this holy <hi type="italic">terumah</hi> on all four sides is then given; and lastly, the command is repeated, that the sanctuary of Jehovah is to be in the centre of it. In <reference osisRef="Ezek.48.11">Eze 48:11</reference>, המקדּשׁ is rendered in the plural by the lxx, Chald. and Syr., and is taken in a distributive sense by Kimchi and others: to the priests whoever is sanctified of the sons of Zadok. This is required by the position of the participle between לכּהנים and מבּני צדוק (compare <reference osisRef="2Chr.26.18">2Ch 26:18</reference>, and for the singular of the participle after a previous plural, <reference osisRef="Ps.8.9">Psa 8:9</reference>). The other rendering, “for the priests is it sanctified, those of the sons of Zadok,” is at variance not only with the position of the words, but also with the fact, namely, that the assignment to the priests of a heave set apart for Jehovah is never designated as קדּשׁ, and from the nature of the case could not be so designated. The apodosis to <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ezek.48.11">Eze 48:11</reference></hi> follows in <reference osisRef="Ezek.48.12">Eze 48:12</reference>, where לכּהנים is resumed in להם. תּרוּמיּה is an adjective formation derived from תּרוּמה, with the signification of an abstract: that which is lifted (the lifting) from the heave, as it were “a terumah in the second potency” (for these formations, see Ewald, §§164 and 165). This <hi type="italic">terumiyah</hi> is called most holy, in contrast with the Levites’ portion of the <hi type="italic">terumah</hi>, which was קדשׁ (<reference osisRef="Ezek.48.14">Eze 48:14</reference>). The priests’ portion is to be beside the territory of the Levites, whether on the southern or northern side cannot be gathered from these words any more than from the definition in <reference osisRef="Ezek.48.13">Eze 48:13</reference> : “and the Levites beside (parallel with) the territory of the priests.” Both statements simply affirm that the portions of the priests and Levites were to lie side by side, and not to be separated by the town possession. - <reference osisRef="Ezek.48.13">Eze 48:13</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ezek.48.14">Eze 48:14</reference> treat of the Levites’ portion: <reference osisRef="Ezek.48.13">Eze 48:13</reference>, of its situation and extent; <reference osisRef="Ezek.48.14">Eze 48:14</reference>, of its law of tenure. The seemingly tautological repetition of the measurement of the length and breadth, as “all the length and the breadth,” is occasioned by the fact “that Ezekiel intends to express himself more briefly here, and not, as in <reference osisRef="Ezek.48.10">Eze 48:10</reference>, to take all the four points of the compass singly; in 'all the length' he embraces the two long sides of the oblong, and in '(all) the breadth' the two broad sides, and affirms that 'all the length,' i.e., of both the north and south sides, is to be twenty-five thousand rods, and 'all the breadth,' i.e., of both the east and west sides, is to be ten thousand rods” (Kliefoth). Hitzig has missed the sense, and therefore proposes to alter the text. With regard to the possession of the Levites, the instructions given in <reference osisRef="Lev.25.34">Lev 25:34</reference> for the field of the Levites’ cities - namely, that none of it was to be sold - are extended to the whole of the territory of the Levites: no part of it is to be alienated by sale or barter. And the character of the possession is assigned as the reason: the first-fruit of the land, i.e., the land lifted off (separated) as first-fruit, is not to pass into the possession of others, because as such it is holy to the Lord. The <hi type="italic">Chetib</hi> ya`abowr יעבור is the correct reading: to pass over, <hi type="italic">sc</hi>. to others, to non-Levites. <div eID="gen15373" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15374" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Ezek.48.15-Ezek.48.18">Eze 48:15-18</reference> treat of the city possession. As the <hi type="italic">terumah</hi> was twenty-five thousand rods in breadth (<reference osisRef="Ezek.48.8">Eze 48:8</reference>), after measuring off ten thousand rods in breadth for the priests and ten thousand rods in breadth for the Levites from the entire breadth, there still remain five thousand rods על, in front of, i.e., along, the long side, which was twenty-five thousand rods. This remnant was to be חל, i.e., common (not holy) land for the city (Jerusalem). למושׁב, for dwelling-places, i.e., for building dwelling-houses upon; and למגרשׁ, for open space, the precinct around the city. The city was to stand in the centre of this oblong. <reference osisRef="Ezek.48.16">Eze 48:16</reference> gives the size of the city: on each of the four sides, four thousand five hundred rods (the חמשׁ, designated by the Masoretes as כתיב ולא קרי, has crept into the text through a copyist’s error); and <reference osisRef="Ezek.48.17">Eze 48:17</reference>, the extent of the open space surrounding it: on each side two hundred and fifty rods. This gives for the city, together with the open space, a square of five thousand rods on every side; so that the city with its precinct filled the entire breadth of the space left for it, and there only remained on the east and west an open space of ten thousand rods in length and five thousand rods in breadth along the holy <hi type="italic">terumah</hi>. This is noticed in <reference osisRef="Ezek.48.18">Eze 48:18</reference>; its produce was to serve for bread, i.e., for maintenance, for the labourers of the city (the masculine suffix in תּבוּאתה refers grammatically to הנּותר). By עבדי העיר Hitzig would understand the inhabitants of the city, because one cultivates a piece of land even by dwelling on it. But this use of עבד cannot be established. Nor are עבדי העיר the workmen employed in building the city, as Gesenius, Hävernick, and others suppose; for the city was not perpetually being built, so that there should be any necessity for setting apart a particular piece of land for the builders; but they are the working men of the city, the labouring class living in the city. They are not to be without possession in the future Jerusalem, but are to receive a possession in land for their maintenance. We are told in <reference osisRef="Ezek.48.19">Eze 48:19</reference> who these workmen are. Here העבד is used collectively: as for the labouring class of the city, people out of all the tribes of Israel shall work upon the land belonging to the city. The suffix in יעבדוּהוּ points back to הנּותר. The transitive explanation, to employ a person in work, has nothing in the language to confirm it. The fact itself is in harmony with the statement in <reference osisRef="Ezek.45.6">Eze 45:6</reference>, that the city was to belong to all Israel. Lastly, in <reference osisRef="Ezek.48.20">Eze 48:20</reference> the dimensions of the whole <hi type="italic">terumah</hi>, and the relation of the city possession to the holy <hi type="italic">terumah</hi>, are given. כּל־התּרוּמה is the whole heave, so far as it has hitherto been described, embracing the property of the priests, of the Levites, and of the city. In this extent it is twenty-five thousand rods long and the same broad. If, however, we add the property of the prince, which is not treated of till <reference osisRef="Ezek.48.21-Ezek.48.23">Eze 48:21-23</reference>, it is considerably longer, and reaches, as has been stated in <reference osisRef="Ezek.48.8">Eze 48:8</reference>, to the boundaries of the land both on the east and west, the Jordan and the Mediterranean Sea, as the several tribe-territories do. But if we omit the prince’s land, the space set apart fro the city possession occupied the fourth part of the holy <hi type="italic">terumah</hi>, i.e., of the portion of the priests and Levites. This is the meaning of the second half of <reference osisRef="Ezek.48.20">Eze 48:20</reference>, which literally reads thus: “to a fourth shall ye lift off the holy <hi type="italic">terumah</hi> for the city possession.” This is not to be understood as meaning that a fourth was to be taken from the holy <hi type="italic">terumah</hi> for the city possession; for that would yield an incorrect proportion, as the twenty thousand rods in breadth would be reduced to fifteen thousand rods by the subtraction of the fourth part, which would be opposed to <reference osisRef="Ezek.48.9">Eze 48:9</reference> and Eze 48:15. The meaning is rather the following: from the whole <hi type="italic">terumah</hi> the fourth part of the area of the holy <hi type="italic">terumah</hi> is to be taken off for the city possession, i.e., five thousand rods for twenty thousand. According to <reference osisRef="Ezek.48.15">Eze 48:15</reference>, this was the size of the domain set apart for the city. <div eID="gen15374" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15375" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Ezek.48.21-Ezek.48.23">Eze 48:21-23</reference> the situation and extent of the prince’s possession are described. For <reference osisRef="Ezek.48.21">Eze 48:21</reference>, vid., Eze 45:7. הנּותר, the rest of the <hi type="italic">terumah</hi>, as it has been defined in <reference osisRef="Ezek.48.8">Eze 48:8</reference>, reaching in length from the Jordan to the Mediterranean. As the holy <hi type="italic">terumah</hi> and the city possession were only twenty-five thousand rods in length, and did not reach to the Jordan on the east, or to the sea on the west, there still remained an area on either side whose length or extent toward the east and west is not given in rods, but may be calculated from the proportion which the intervening <hi type="italic">terumah</hi> bore to the length of the land (from east to west). אל־פּני and על־פּני, in front of, or along, the front of the twenty-five thousand rods, refer to the eastern and western boundaries of the <hi type="italic">terumah</hi>, which was twenty-five thousand rods in length. In <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ezek.48.21">Eze 48:21</reference></hi> the statement is repeated, that the holy <hi type="italic">terumah</hi> and the sanctuary were to lie in the centre of it, i.e., between the portions of land appointed for the prince on either side; and lastly, in <reference osisRef="Ezek.48.22">Eze 48:22</reference> it is still further stated, with regard to the prince’s land on both sides of the <hi type="italic">terumah</hi>, that it was to lie between the adjoining tribe-territories of Judah (to the north) and Benjamin (to the south), so that it was to be bounded by these two. But this is expressed in a heavy and therefore obscure manner. The words בּתוך אשׁר לנשׂיא יהיה, “in the centre of that which belongs to the prince,” belong to העיר... וּמאחזּת, and form together with the latter the subject, which is written absolutely; so that מן is not used in a partitive, but in a local sense (from), and the whole is to be rendered thus: And as for that which lies on the side of the possession of the Levites, and of the possession of the city in the centre of what belongs to the prince, (that which lies) between the territory of Judah and the territory of Benjamin shall belong to the prince. Hitzig’s explanation - what remains between Judah and Benjamin, from the city territory to the priests’ domain, both inclusive, shall belong to the prince - is arbitrary, and perverts the sense. The periphrastic designation of the <hi type="italic">terumah</hi> bounded off between the prince’s land by the two portions named together without a copula, viz., “possession of the Levites and possession of the city,” is worthy of notice. This periphrasis of the whole by two portions, shows that the portions named formed the boundaries of the whole, that the third portion, which is not mentioned, was enclosed within the two, so that the priests’ portion with the sanctuary lay between them. - In <reference osisRef="Ezek.48.23-Ezek.48.27">Eze 48:23-27</reference> the rest of the tribes located to the south of the <hi type="italic">terumah</hi> are mentioned in order; and in <reference osisRef="Ezek.48.28">Eze 48:28</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ezek.48.29">Eze 48:29</reference> the account of the division of the land is brought to a close with a repetition of the statement as to the southern boundary (cf. <reference osisRef="Ezek.47.19">Eze 47:19</reference>), and a comprehensive concluding formula. <div eID="gen15375" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15376" type="x-p"/> If now we attempt, in order to form a clear idea of the relation in which this prophetic division of the land stands to the actual size of Canaan according to the boundaries described in Eze 47:15., to determine the length and breadth of the <hi type="italic">terumah</hi> given here by their geographical dimensions, twenty-five thousand rods, according to the metrological calculations of Boeckh and Bertheau, would be 10·70 geographical miles, or, according to the estimate of the Hebrew cubit by Thenius, only 9·75 geographical miles.<note placement="foot">According to Boeckh, one sacred cubit was equal to 234-1/3 Paris lines = 528.62 millimètres; according to Thenius = 214-1/2 P. l. = 481.62 millim. Now as one geographical mile, the 5400th part of the circumference of the globe, which is 40,000,000 metres, is equivalent to 7407.398 metres = 22, 803.290 old Paris feet, the geographical mile according to Boeckh is 14, 012-1/10 cubits = 2335-1/2 rods (sacred measure); according to Thenius, 15, 380-1/6 cubits = 2563-1/3 roads (s. m.), from which the numbers given in the text may easily be calculated.</note> <div eID="gen15376" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15377" type="x-p"/> The extent of Canaan from Beersheba, or Kadesh, up to a line running across from Râs esh-Shukah to the spring El Lebweh, is 3 1/3 degrees, i.e., fifty geographical miles, ten of which are occupied by the <hi type="italic">terumah</hi>, and forty remain for the twelve tribe-territories, so that each tribe-lot would be 3 1/3 geographical miles in breadth. If, now, we reckon three geographical miles as the breadth of each of the five tribe-lots to the south of the <hi type="italic">terumah</hi>, and as the land becomes broader toward the south a breadth of 3-4/7 geographical miles for the seven tribe-lots to the north, the <hi type="italic">terumah</hi> set apart in the centre of the land would extend from the site of Jerusalem to Dothan or Jenin. If, however, we take into consideration the breadth of the land from east to west in the neighbourhood of Jerusalem, or where the Jordan enters the Dead Sea, Canaan is eleven geographical miles in breadth, whereas at Jenin it is hardly ten geographical miles broad. If, therefore, the length of the <hi type="italic">terumah</hi> (from east to west) was fully ten geographical miles, there would only remain a piece of land of half a mile in breadth on the east and west at the southern boundary, and nothing at all at the northern, for prince’s land. We have therefore given to the <hi type="italic">terumah</hi> upon the map (Plate IV) the length and breadth of eight geographical miles, which leaves a tract of two miles on the average for the prince’s land, so that it would occupy a fifth of the area of the holy <hi type="italic">terumah</hi>, whereas the city possession covered a fourth. No doubt the breadth of the <hi type="italic">terumah</hi> from south to north is also diminished thereby, so that it cannot have reached quite down to Jerusalem or quite up to Jenin. - If, now, we consider that the distances of places, and therefore also the measurements of a land in length and breadth, are greater in reality than those given upon the map, on account partly of the mountains and valleys and partly of the windings of the roads, and, still further, that our calculations of the Hebrew cubit are not quite certain, and that even the smaller estimates of Thenius are possibly still too high, the measurements of the <hi type="italic">terumah</hi> given by Ezekiel correspond as exactly to the actual size of the land of Canaan as could be expected with a knowledge of its extent obtained not by trigonometrical measurement, but from a simple calculation of the length of the roads. - But this furnishes a confirmation by no means slight of our assumption, that the lengths and breadths indicated here are measured by rods and not by cubits. Reckoned by cubits, the <hi type="italic">terumah</hi> would be only a mile and a half or a mile and two-thirds in length and breadth, and the city possession would be only a third of a mile broad; whereas the prince’s land would be more than six times as large as the whole of the <hi type="italic">terumah</hi>, - i.e., of the territory of the Levites, the priests, and the city, - thirteen times as large as the priests’ land, and from thirty to thirty-two times as large as the city possession = proportions the improbability of which is at once apparent.
entries.52b8af06cd20589ddf87a41e65f38d66a59c4506: <reference osisRef="Ezek.48.30-Ezek.48.35">Eze 48:30-35</reference> <div eID="gen15377" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Size, Gates, and Name of the City</title> <div sID="gen15378" type="x-p"/> To complete the whole picture of the future land of Israel, what has been stated in <reference osisRef="Ezek.48.15">Eze 48:15</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ezek.48.16">Eze 48:16</reference> concerning the size of the holy city is still further expanded here. - Eze 48:30. <hi type="italic">And these are the outgoings of the city from the north side, four thousand and five hundred (rods) measurement.</hi> Eze 48:31. <hi type="italic">And the gates of the city according to the names of the tribes of Israel: three gates toward the north; the gate of Reuben one, the gate of Judah one, the gate of Levi one.</hi> Eze 48:32. <hi type="italic">And on the east side four thousand five hundred (rods): and three gates; namely, the gate of Joseph one, the gate of Benjamin one, the gate of Dan one.</hi> Eze 48:33. <hi type="italic">And to the south side, four thousand five hundred measurement: and three gates; the gate of Simeon one, the gate of Issachar one, the gate of Zebulon one.</hi> Eze 48:34. <hi type="italic">To the west side, four thousand five hundred - their gates three; the gate of Gad one, the gate of Asher one, the gate of Naphtali one.</hi> Eze 48:35. <hi type="italic">Round about, eighteen thousand (rods); and the name of the city: from henceforth Jehovah there.</hi> - The situation of the city of God within the terumah and its external dimensions have already been generally indicated in <reference osisRef="Ezek.48.15">Eze 48:15</reference>, Eze 48:16. Here the measurement of the several sides is specified with a notice of their gates, and this is preceded by the heading, “the outlets of the city.” תּוצאת, the outgoings (not extensions, for the word never has this meaning) as the furthest extremities in which a city or a tract of land terminates; not outlets or gates, which are expressly distinguished from them, but outgoing sides; hence the definition of the extent or length of the several sides is appended immediately afterwards. The enumeration commences, as above in the case of the land, with the north side. Each side has three gates, so that the whole city has twelve, which bear the names of the twelve tribes, like the gates of the heavenly Jerusalem in <reference osisRef="Rev.21.12">Rev 21:12</reference>, because it will be the city of the true people of God. Levi is included here, and consequently Ephraim and Manasseh are united in the one tribe of Joseph. The three sons of Leah commence the series with the northern gates. They also stand first in the blessing of Moses in <reference osisRef="Deut.33.6-Deut.33.8">Deu 33:6-8</reference> : the first-born in age, the first-born by virtue of the patriarchal blessing, and the one chosen by Jehovah for His own service in the place of the first-born. Then follow, for the eastern gates, the two sons of Rachel, according to their age (thus deviating from <reference osisRef="Deut.33.12">Deu 33:12</reference> and <reference osisRef="Deut.33.13">Deu 33:13</reference>), and, along with them, the elder son of Rachel’s maid; for the southern gates, the three other sons of Leah; and lastly, for the western gates, the three other sons of the maids. Being thus indicated by the names of its gates as the city of all Israel, the city itself receives a name, which exalts it into the city of God (Jehovah). But different explanations have been given of the words in <reference osisRef="Ezek.48.35">Eze 48:35</reference> which refer to this name. The allusion in מיום and the meaning of שׁמּה are both disputed points. It is true that the latter literally means “thither;” but Ezekiel also uses it as synonymous with שׁם, “there,” in <reference osisRef="Ezek.23.3">Eze 23:3</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ezek.32.29-Ezek.32.30">Eze 32:29-30</reference>, so that the assertion that שׁמּה never means “there” is incorrect. מיום, from day forward, equivalent to henceforward; but not henceforth and for ever, though this may be implied in the context. Whether מיום be taken in connection with the preceding words, “the name of the city will henceforward be,” or with those which follow, the name of the city will be, “henceforward Jehovah there,” makes no material difference so far as the thought is concerned, as the city can only bear the name from the time when Jehovah is שׁמּה, and can only bear it so long as Jehovah is שׁמּה. But so far as the question is concerned, whether שׁמּה signifies thither or there in this passage, Hävernick is of opinion, indeed, that the whole of Ezekiel’s vision does not harmonize with the meaning “there,” inasmuch as he separates temple and city, so that Jehovah does not properly dwell in Jerusalem, but, in the strictest an highest sense, in His sanctuary, and turns thence to Jerusalem with the fulness of His grace and love. But if Jehovah does not merely direct His love toward the city from afar off, but, as Hävernick still further says, turns it fully toward it, causes His good pleasure to rest upon it, then He also rules and is in the city with His love, so that it can bear the name “Jehovah thither (there).” In any case, the interpretation, “Jehovah will from henceforth proceed thither, to restore it, to make it a holy city” (Kliefoth), is untenable; for the name is not given to Jerusalem when lying waste, but to the city already restored and fully built, which Ezekiel sees in the spirit. He has therefore before this turned His favour once more to Jerusalem, which was laid waste; and the name יהוה שׁמּה, given to the new Jerusalem, can only affirm that henceforward it is to be a city of Jehovah, i.e., that from this time forth Jehovah will be and rule in her. The rendering “Jehovah thither” does not answer to this, but only the rendering, “Jehovah will be there.” compare <reference osisRef="Isa.60.14">Isa 60:14</reference>, where Jerusalem is called the city of Jehovah, Zion of the Holy One in Israel, because the glory of Jehovah has risen over her as a brilliant light.  <chapter eID="Ezek.48"/> <div eID="gen15378" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen14755" osisID="Ezek" type="book"/>
